amendments.rule: A pronominal suffix aligns to the English pronoun that realizes it, which is usually a possessive or object pronoun: `מִינֵהוּ` → *his kind* splits into the noun and *his*. **Where the ASV's paraphrase realizes one suffix twice, both pronouns belong to that suffix's one possibly discontinuous unit; an earlier realization does not make the later one `added`.** `מִכֶּם מָזוֹר` → *cure you of your wound* gives *you ... your* to the suffix and heads on *you*, the direct pronoun rather than the possessive recasting. **Where the ASV intensifies a possessive with *own*, the whole emphatic possessive belongs to the suffix:** `דְּרָכֶיךָ` → *thine own ways* gives *thine own* to the suffix and *ways* to the noun, headed on *thine*; do not attach *own* to the host noun merely because it stands beside it. **Where the ASV replaces the suffix's ordinary pronoun with a lexical nominal expression naming its referent, that whole expression realizes the suffix and the supplied lexical antecedent is not `added`; head on the noun or name that carries the referent.** `נְחָלֶיהָ` → *the streams of Edom* gives *of Edom* to the suffix and heads on *Edom*, and the suffix in `בִּסְעִיפֶיהָ הַפֹּרִיָּה` → *in the outmost branches of a fruitful tree* takes *of a tree*, headed on *tree*, while the adjective keeps *fruitful*. **An independent personal pronoun the ASV renders the same way goes with it.** Where a written subject or object pronoun is realized not by an English pronoun but by a demonstrative with a supplied lexical noun naming its referent, that whole expression realizes the pronoun and the supplied noun is not `added`; head on the noun carrying the referent: `הִיא הַסִּיר` → ***this city*** *is the caldron* gives *this city* to `הִיא`, exactly as rule 20's identifying formula gives *These ... that* to a `הוּא`, and an ASV italic on the supplied noun corroborates it without deciding it, by rule 7. Where the referent's own noun stands written in the clause, the pronoun takes only the determiner the ASV writes for it and the article is `unrepresented` under rule 41's limit: `הִיא נִתְּנָה הָאָרֶץ` → ***this*** *land* *is given*. **Where the ASV expands an object suffix into a full nominal expression containing a pronoun, the whole expression may realize the suffix, but the target head remains the pronoun that directly realizes the suffix's lexeme:** `אֲשִׁיבֶנּוּ` → *I will turn away the punishment thereof* gives *the punishment thereof* to the suffix and heads on *thereof*, not on the generic noun *punishment*. All eight occurrences of this prophetic formula across Amos 1–2 follow that analysis. **An English relative pronoun may be what realizes a suffix.** Where the ASV recasts the suffix's own clause as a relative clause modifying the noun its referent names, the relative — *that*, *which*, *who*, *whom* — is the pronoun the suffix is rendered by and joins its unit, exactly as rule 17 gives the *which* of such a recasting to an explicit subject pronoun, and whatever preposition the suffix stands on keeps only what the recasting leaves it under rules 40, 43 and 49: `שָׂרִים זָהָב לָהֶם` → *princes* ***that*** *had gold* gives *had* to the possessive `לְ` under rule 43 and *that* to the suffix, and `וַיָּסֶךְ אֱלוֹהַּ בַּעֲדוֹ` → *And* ***whom*** *God hath hedged in* gives *whom* to the suffix and leaves `בַּעַד` `unrepresented` under rule 40. Such a relative is not a subordinator supplied for the clause: rules 46 and 55 govern a clause with no morpheme in it to answer for the word, and here the suffix answers for it, so read whether a pronominal morpheme stands in the clause before marking a relative `added`. Where no suffix or other possessive morpheme is present, a supplied possessive expression such as *your own* or *thine own* answers to no source morpheme and is `added` under rule 30. **The suffix on an infinitive construct is that infinitive's subject and takes the English subject pronoun the ASV writes for it**, while the infinitive keeps the verb: `עַד כַּלֹּתוֹ אֹתְךָ` → *until he have consumed thee* gives *he* to the suffix and *have consumed* to the infinitive, and the object marker and its own suffix are read separately by rules 16 and 11. The ASV's pronoun need not agree in number with the suffix — `עַד הַאֲבִידוֹ אֹתָךְ` → *until they have caused thee to perish* — because the English subject answers to the referent the translation has in view; align the pronoun that is written. This governs only a suffix that is actually present: where none is, a subject pronoun the ASV supplies for an infinitive belongs to the infinitive itself under rules 48 and 52, and rules 40 and 43 dispose of the other places where the English pronoun realizing a morpheme is neither possessive nor object.
amendments.why: JOB.3.15 (`שָׂרִים זָהָב לָהֶם` → *princes that had gold*) and JOB.3.23 (`בַּעֲדוֹ` → *whom*) both write an English relative where no relative morpheme stands but a suffix does. Rule 18's enumeration ran only to possessive and object pronouns, with rules 40 and 43 catching subject pronouns, so a later pass reading rule 46's closing paragraph or rule 55's count would mark these `added` and the suffix `unrepresented` — an added and an unrepresented where one written morpheme plainly answers for the word. Rule 17 already gives such a recasting's *which* to an explicit subject pronoun, and the corpus aligns a pronominal suffix to *whose* in 65 units with no relative morpheme present, so the extension is the same reading and does not contradict anything below. Scoped tightly to a relative that fills the slot the suffix's own pronoun would occupy, and it explicitly leaves rules 46 and 55 governing the clause where no pronominal morpheme stands, which is how this chapter marked three supplied relatives `added` in 3.3, 3.16 and 3.25.

amendments.rule: The article `הַ` aligns to English *the*. Hebrew has no indefinite article, so an English *a* or *an* belongs to the noun that licenses it and is not `added`. **The same ownership applies to a definite article the ASV supplies where no Hebrew article morpheme is present:** it belongs to the nominal expression it determines and is not `added`. **And it applies to a supplied quantifying determiner such as *any*, which is the word English writes in that same slot where *a* will not stand — under a negation, in a question, or after a comparative.** Where a bare noun carries no determiner morpheme of its own and the ASV writes an *any* before it, that word determines the nominal expression exactly as a supplied *a* or *the* does: it joins the noun's unit, is not `added`, and is never the head, which stays on the word carrying the lexeme under rule 31 — `לִמְלָאכָה` → *for any work* gives *for* to the preposition and *any work* to the noun, headed on *work*. **But only where no morpheme in the clause licenses that determiner.** A `כֹּל` standing on the noun is itself what the *any* renders and takes it, the noun keeping only its own word — `כָּל־עֵץ` → *any tree*, `כָּל־כְּלִי` → *any vessel* — and where the ASV recasts a clause's negation onto a nominal standing in it, the negative takes the determiner that negation has become. **Read which nominal the ASV has put the determiner on rather than what its grammatical role is**: an object takes it in `לֹא יֵעָשֶׂה לִמְלָאכָה` → *it was meet for* ***no*** *work*, which gives *no* to `לֹא`, discontinuous from the verb it negates under rule 25, and leaves `מְלָאכָה` the bare *work*; a subject takes it in `אַל־תָּבֹא רְנָנָה בוֹ` → *Let* ***no*** *joyful voice come therein*, which gives *no* to `אַל` and leaves the noun its own *joyful voice*. A jussive or prohibitive `אַל` is read on the same terms as `לֹא`. Count the determiners and read which morpheme each answers to, as rule 41 counts a phrase's determiners and rule 29 counts its *the*s. This does not reach a supplied possessive, which rule 18 leaves `added` where no suffix or other possessive morpheme is present. **For Aramaic, a separately segmented determined-state ending (`Td`) is treated likewise:** align it to *the* when the ASV writes a corresponding article, and mark it `unrepresented` under rule 29 when the ASV writes no separate article, including where another determiner supplies the determination. More specific construct and substantival rules still decide which source unit inside that expression takes it.
amendments.why: JOB.3.7's `אַל־תָּבֹא רְנָנָה בוֹ` → *Let no joyful voice come therein* recasts the negation onto the clause's subject, which rule 15's clause did not reach: it said 'onto its object'. Read literally, a pass would instead treat *no* as a determiner supplied for the noun and fold it into `רְנָנָה`'s unit — a different unit membership for a word the negative morpheme plainly is. The widening changes nothing about the object case, which keeps its own example and its rule 25 note, and adds only that the nominal's role does not decide it; the corpus's 247 `לֹא` → *no* units are consistent with either role, so nothing below is contradicted. The `אַל` sentence is stated because this chapter's four occurrences are all jussive negatives and the rule's only example was `לֹא`.

conventions: Supplied English relatives are triaged by what stands in the Hebrew clause, not by whether the antecedent is written: a relative the ASV supplies for a finite clause juxtaposed to a written antecedent with no relative and no pronominal morpheme in it is `added` (3.3 *the night which said*, 3.16 *infants that never saw light*, 3.25 *the thing which I fear*); a written כִּי or אֲשֶׁר takes it (3.12, 3.25b); a pronominal suffix the recasting makes the relative clause's subject or object takes it (3.15 *that had gold*, 3.23 *whom ... hedged in*); and an anarthrous participle or adjective takes it into its own unit under rule 46 (3.5, 3.8, 3.17, 3.19, 3.20, 3.22).

In the demonstrative phrase הַ + noun + הַ + הוּא (3.4, 3.6, 3.7) the pronoun takes the ASV's *that* under rule 41's limit, since a written morpheme licenses the determiner, and both articles are `unrepresented`, the ASV writing no *the* for the phrase. This is the source of the six Td disagreements with BSB, which attaches *that* to the article; the corpus also records a competing noncompositional fusion of הַ+הוּא, so the reading was taken deliberately rather than by default.

English the ASV supplies by ellipsis from a neighbouring verse's parallel line is `added`: the *There* of 3.18, carried from the two שָׁם of 3.17, and the italic *Why is light given* of 3.23, carried from 3.20. Rule 10 confines the verse, so no morpheme in the verse licenses such a word; this is not rule 34's gapping, which supplies a copula inside the verse being aligned.

Rule 44's bare-object clause is applied to a pronominal object suffix as to a bare object noun: where the English verb reaches a suffix through a preposition the ASV has written and no marker or preposition of the object's own stands, the preposition joins the verb's unit — *seek for it* (3.4), *seize upon it* (3.6), *dig for it* (3.21), *cometh upon me* (3.25) — the suffix keeping only its pronoun.

report: Read all 26 verses end to end alongside the 24-lemma candidate table. No construction is analysed two ways without something in the source licensing the difference, so patches is empty.

Supplied relative pronouns are the chapter's one real risk, and the table is blind to three of them because they are `added`. The triage is uniform: `added` where no morpheme stands (3.3 *which*, 3.16 *that*, 3.25 first line *which*); the written morpheme's where one does (3.12 כִּי takes *that*, 3.25 second line אֲשֶׁר takes *that which*, and the pronominal suffixes of 3.15 *princes that had gold* and 3.23 *whom God hath hedged in*); rule 46's where the head is an anarthrous participle or adjective (3.5, 3.8, 3.17, 3.19, 3.20, 3.22). The two suffix cases are what this chapter taught and are returned as an amendment to rule 18.

Heads on one-substantive-to-two-word phrases run rule 31's subtraction in both directions: *untimely birth*, *joyful voice*, *waste places*, *man child* head on the distinguishing word, while *thick darkness* and *hid treasures* head on the noun that already names the thing. Two directions, one test — this is the table's loudest false positive and it is licensed each time.

הַ...הַהוּא is uniform in 3.4, 3.6 and 3.7: the demonstrative pronoun takes *that* under rule 41's limit and both articles go unrepresented. That accounts for 6 of the 12 BSB disagreements. The corpus records a competing noncompositional fusion of הַ+הוּא to *that* in 4 units, so this is logged as a convention and deliberately not promoted.

BSB: no genuine error. Td x6 is the demonstrative convention; 3.9 בְּ and 3.23 בַּעֲד are rule 40 recastings (*behold the eyelids* promotes the object; *hedged in* is verb-plus-particle under rule 44); 3.11 and 3.25 waws have no connective written for them; 3.17 כֹחַ is a rectum the ASV leaves unwritten; 3.19 הוּא is a copular pronoun whose *are* rule 20 sends to the locative predicate שָׁם. No accepted edge was changed.

Two ASV supplies carried over from a neighbouring verse are `added` (3.18 *There* from 3.17's two שָׁם, 3.23 *Why is light given* from 3.20). Rule 10 forces this — the licensing morpheme is in another verse — and Job's parallelism will keep producing it, so it is recorded as a convention.

Minor, left unpatched: the 3.17 note for כֹחַ cites rule 22 for a rectum the ASV simply does not write, where rule 22 is about a repeated element. The status and edges are right; only the citation is loose.
